title: How a web page loads
intro: Click the outlined box to go to the next step. Open "How it works" for the detail.

start.title: Start here
start.summary: Click the outlined box to follow how a web page reaches your screen.

end.title: That’s the whole trip
end.summary: Seven steps, usually finished in under a second. Click any box to revisit it.

steps.label: DNS lookup
steps.title: Find the address
steps.summary: Your browser needs the server’s IP address, so it looks up the domain name.

items.heading: Browser cache
items.text: If you visited the site recently, the browser already has the address and skips the lookup entirely.

items.heading: Operating system and router
items.text: Next it asks the OS resolver, which checks its own cache and the hosts file. Many home routers cache answers too.

items.heading: Recursive resolver
items.text: Still nothing? The question goes to a resolver run by your ISP or a public one like 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8, which does the legwork for you.

items.heading: Root, TLD, authoritative
items.text: The resolver asks a root server, which points to the .com servers, which point to the site’s own nameservers. Those hold the real answer.

items.heading: Answer with a TTL
items.text: An A record (IPv4) or AAAA record (IPv6) comes back with a time-to-live that says how long everyone may cache it.

steps.example:
example.com.   300   IN   A   93.184.215.14
# name          TTL  class type address

steps.label: Handshake
steps.title: Open a secure line
steps.summary: Browser and server connect and agree on encryption before any data moves.

items.heading: TCP handshake
items.text: SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. One round trip that confirms both sides can send and receive.

items.heading: ClientHello
items.text: The browser lists the TLS versions and ciphers it supports and sends its half of a key exchange.

items.heading: ServerHello and certificate
items.text: The server picks the cipher, sends its half of the key exchange, and proves its identity with a certificate.

items.heading: Certificate check
items.text: The browser verifies the certificate chains to a trusted authority, matches the domain, and hasn’t expired.

items.heading: Session keys
items.text: Both sides derive the same secret keys without ever sending them. With TLS 1.3 this takes one round trip. HTTP/3 folds TCP and TLS into a single QUIC handshake.

steps.example:
client → SYN
server ← SYN-ACK
client → ACK
client → ClientHello      (versions, ciphers, key share)
server ← ServerHello      (choice, key share, certificate)
both   ↔ encrypted from here on

steps.label: HTTP request
steps.title: Ask for the page
steps.summary: The browser sends an HTTP GET request for the page you asked for.

items.heading: Method and path
items.text: GET asks to read a resource. The path is everything after the domain, here just / for the homepage.

items.heading: Headers
items.text: Metadata about the request: which host, which formats and languages the browser accepts, what software it is.

items.heading: Cookies
items.text: If you’ve logged in before, a session cookie rides along so the server knows who you are.

items.heading: Over the wire
items.text: HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 send the same information as compact binary frames and let many requests share one connection.

steps.example:
GET / HTTP/1.1
Host: example.com
Accept: text/html
Accept-Language: en
Cookie: session=8f2c…

steps.label: Server responds
steps.title: Server does the work
steps.summary: The server works out what to send and builds the response.

items.heading: Edge cache
items.text: A CDN close to you may already hold a copy of the page and answer in milliseconds without touching the origin.

items.heading: Load balancer
items.text: Otherwise the request is routed to one of many identical app servers so no single machine is overwhelmed.

items.heading: Application logic
items.text: The app matches the path to a route, checks your session, and queries the database for the content it needs.

items.heading: Render
items.text: The data is poured into a template to produce the final HTML.

items.heading: Response
items.text: A status code, headers that describe the content and how to cache it, then the body, usually compressed.

steps.example:
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8
Content-Encoding: br
Cache-Control: max-age=60

<!doctype html>…

steps.label: Browser parses
steps.title: Read the blueprint
steps.summary: The browser reads the HTML and gathers everything the page needs.

items.heading: Build the DOM
items.text: HTML is parsed as it streams in, turning tags into a tree of nodes. The browser doesn’t wait for the whole file.

items.heading: Preload scanner
items.text: A second, lightweight parser skims ahead to find images, styles and scripts so their downloads start early.

items.heading: CSS becomes the CSSOM
items.text: Stylesheets are parsed into their own tree. Rendering waits for them so you don’t see unstyled content.

items.heading: Scripts
items.text: A plain script pauses parsing while it downloads and runs. defer and async scripts let parsing continue.

items.heading: Everything else
items.text: Images and fonts download in parallel and slot in as they arrive.

steps.label: Page painted
steps.title: Paint the pixels
steps.summary: The page structure and styles combine into what you actually see.

items.heading: Render tree
items.text: DOM and CSSOM are combined into a tree of only what will be visible. Elements with display: none are left out.

items.heading: Layout
items.text: The browser calculates the exact size and position of every box on the page.

items.heading: Paint
items.text: Each box is filled in: text, colours, borders, images, drawn into separate layers.

items.heading: Composite
items.text: The GPU stacks the layers into the final frame. Animating transform or opacity only redoes this step, which is why it’s cheap.

items.heading: First paint
items.text: The moment content first appears is the first contentful paint, a key measure of how fast a page feels.
